INTRODUCTION This manual! offers general !zed troubleshooting procedures for common types of mal functtons which can be appiled to most video games. We wil! not attempt to give you specific Instructions for troubleshooting particular games because thls would Involve hundreds of pages of more repetitive Instructions, differing only In the specific detalls of each game, The most common problems occur in harness components such as the coln acceptor, player con- trols, Interconnecting wiring, etc. These areas are covered In moderate detall. The TV Monitor and Game Logie Printed Circult Boards (PCB's) provide their fair share of problems too, but not to the extent of the harness and. I+s component parts. As you already know, the Game Logle PC Boards are complex devices. Each contalns a great number of different interrelated circults. The major changes which give each game Its own particular Individuality are accomp!Ished In the EPROMS and other IntIgrated CIrcult devices that are Installed on each of these PC Boards. GENERAL TROURLE SHOOTING SUGGESTIONS The first step In troubleshooting Is to correctly Identify the malfunctions symptoms, This Includes not only the clrcults or features malfunctioning, but also those stI!! operation- al. A carefully tralned eye wii! pick up other clues to what's wrong as well. For [n= stance, a game in which the computer functions fall completely just after money was collect= ed may have a quarter shorting the PCR traces. Often an experienced troubleshooter will be able to spot the cause of a problem even before opening the cabinet, After all the clues are carefully considered, the possible malfunctioning areas can be nar- rowed down to one or two good suspects. Those areas can be examined by a process of el|min- ation untl! the cause of the malfunction Is d!scovered. HARNESS COMPONENT TROUBLESHOOTING Typical problems falling In thls category are coin and credit problems, power problems, and failure of Individual features, NO GAME CREDIT - ~ For example, a prospective game player Inserts a quarter or token and Ts not awarded a game, The first thing to check [s whether or not the quarter or token [s returned. {f I+ was returned, the malfunction most certainly !fes In the coln acceptor It- self, First, use a set of test colnms (both old and new) to ascertain that the player's coin Is not understze or underwelght. If your test coins are also returned, coin acceptor seryv- Ictng Is Indicated. Generally, the cause of this particular problem |s a maladjusted magnet gate. Normalty, this will mean slightly closing the magnet gate by turning the adjusting screw out a bit. -6-

{¢ the quarter or token Is not returned and there Is no game credit, the cause of the mal~ function may be In one of several areas. First, try operating the coln return button; If the coln Is returned, the problem Is most !Iikely In the magnet gate. Enlarge the gap ac~ cording the coln acceptor manufacturers service procedures. (tf this does not cure the prob- lem, remove the coln acceptor, clean It, and perform the manufacturers suggested major ad— justment procedure. !f the trapped coln fs not returned when the wiper lever is actuated, you may have an accep- tor jammed by a slug, gummed up with beer, a jammed coin chute, or mechanical fallure of the acceptor mechanism. In this case, first check for the slug that wll! genera!!y be trapped against the magnet. tf a slug Is found, simply remove It and test the acceptor. {f the chute Is blocked, remove the acceptor and remove the jammed coins. If there Is actual fail- ure of the acceptor, remove the unIlt and repair as Indicated by the acceptor manufacturers service procedures. !f the cotn Is making Its way through the acceptor (that Is, falling into the coln box), yet there Is stil! no game credit, you elther have a mechanical fallure of the coln switch or electrical fallure of the coln and credit circults. The first place to begin Is by checking the coln switch. Most of these switches are the make/break variety of micro switch, They are checked for continulty between the "NO", "NC", and "Ct terminals, When not actuated, the "NC'"' and "C" terminals shou!d be continuous and the "NO" terminal open. When actuated, the "NO" and "C" terminals should be continuous and the "NC" terminal open. If the coin switch checks good, Inspect the solder connections to the colin switch terminals to be sure there Is good contact at this point. If necessary, use a continulty tester and check from the terminal lug on the switch to the assoclated PCB trace. This wil! tel! you if there Is a continuous |!ine al! the way to the cred!t clrcult. lf the colIn switch wires do check good, the problem Is In one of the game !ogic boards - = most likeiy In the coln and credit cIrcultry. t# you do get a game credit when a coin Is deposited, but the game wil! not start when the one or two player start button Is pressed, there may be a problem In the start switch, the Interconnect!ng wiring, or the game logic boards. First, check the switch. If the switch Is OK, proceed to check the wiring. Again, make sure you go from the termina! tug on the switch to the PCR trace. ThIs way, you wllf check the terminal contact as wel! as the PCR edge connector contact. If the wiring Is continuous, proceed to check the PCB credit cir= cuit. If not, check each section of the wiring, until! the discontinuity Is located. If the wiring ts OK, the problem must !le In the games logic boards. TRANSFORMER AND LINE VOLTAGE PROBLEMS Your game MUST have the correct IIne voltage to operate properly. If the !Ine voltage drops too low, one of the games logic clIrcults will disable the credit acceptance circult. The point at which the games logic cIrcults wi!! fall to function Is approximately 105 volts AC. Low line voltage may have many causes. LIne voltage normally fluctuates a certain amount during the day as the total usage varles, Peak usage times occur malnt!y at dawn and/or dusk. So If your games problem seems to be related to the time of day, this may be a fac- tor, A large load connected to the same !Ine as the game (such as a farge alr cond!tioner or other device with an exceptionally large electric motor) may drop the IIne voltage s!g- nificantly when starting up. ThIs drop can result In an Intermittent credit problem, In addition, poor connections In the locatlon wiring, plug, or !!ne cord may also cause a sig- niflcant drop In power. Cold solder joints In the games harness, especially In areas !ike the transformer connections, Interlock switch, or fuse block, may a!so produce the same re- sults, although probably on a more permanent basis. -7-

Sometimes location owners (especially In bars) replace light switches with dimmer rheostats, and the game Is sometimes on the same IIne, Obviously, the voltage avallable to the game js going to drop dramatically when the dimmer 1s turned down. In any case, the way to check for proper |Ine voltage Is with your VOM. Set the VOM to the 250 VAC scale and stick the probes Into the wal! outlet the game was connected to. If It's OK here, check the transformer primary connections. {tf you do not get 117 VAC, examine the solder joInts on the transformer, fuse block, and Interlock switch. If you do get 117 VAC, the problem must be elther In the transformer, harness connections, or In the PCB power sup- ply. \# you suspect the transformer, check Its secondaries with the VOM set to the 50 VAC scale and correfate the readings with the legend on the side of the transformer, The transformer must also be correctly grounded, so check the ground potentia!t as wel!, especlatly If there 1s a hum bar rolling up or down the Monitor screen. NO POWER, NO PICTURE - - If the Monitor screen Is completely dark, first look in back of the Monitor to see If the CRT filament Is glowing. [{f It Is, try adjusting the brightness con- trol. tf no luck here, put your ear near the Monitor and IIsten for the high-pitched B+ hum produced by the flyback transformer. If you get the hum but no plieture, and you have tried adjusting the brightness, major Monitor servicing Is Indicated. tf the monttor seems completely dead, check the rest of the game to see If It has power, If It doesn't, go directly to the wall outlet and check there. If OK there, check the game fuse(s), Interlock switch, and Interconnecting wire lengths. Sometimes It Is difficult to tell If a slow=blow fuse has blown. {tf In doubt, check It us- Ing any of the VOM "R" scales. HARNESS PROBLEMS - ~ Other harness problems Include blowing fuses and matfunction!Ing con- trols, The repeating blown-fuse problem can sometimes be quite exasperating to solve. Short cIrcults have the tendency to occur In areas almost Impossible to find. First, try Insert- Ing a new fuse as old fuses age and sometimes hlow without cause. If the new fuse also blows, you definitely have a short. The best way to approach thls problem Is by d!sconnecting devices that may be causIng the problem, such as the TV Monitor, the varlous PCB's one at a time, and the Isolation trans~ former. Disconnect the devices by FIRST turning the game off, disconnecting I+ from its wall outlet. Remove the blown fuse and connect your VOM across the terminals of the fuse block (this wil! save blowing a fuse each time you want to check the cIircult). Set your VOM to one of Its resistance scales. You should be reading a short. If not you probubly have a part that only shorts out after It Is heated up ~ we'l! cover this Im a minute. So, assum- ing you are reading a short on your VOM, disconnect the components from thelr cabling one at a time, checking the VOM after each one Is disconnected. When the short disappears, you have just disconnected the bad component. {f al! components are disconnected and the short still remains, the problem Is In the harness and only patient exploration wil! reveal its location. Carefully examine all the wiring, looking for terminals that may. be touching, metal objects such as colns shorting the connections, or burned Insulation, if necessary, use the VOM to check each suspected wire. -8-

OK, now lets assume that you connected your VOM across the fuse block terminals as stated above and you did not read a short. This most !lkely means that you have a component somewhere In that game that ONLY goes bad AFTER it heats up. {+t checks good when Its cold, In this case, turn the game off and disconnect ALL of Its components. Insta{! a known good fuse In the fuse block. And turn the game on. If the fuse does not blow after a tew minutes, you know that It Is not anything to do with the wire harness. (In this Instance, It shouldn't be, actually, Aut It never hurts to check.) Next, turn the game off again and reconnect ONE component, Turn the game back on and wait a few minutes to see If the fuse blows, If It does not, turn the game off again and reconnect another single component, Turn the game back on and walt a few minutes to see If the fuse blows. Repeat thls proce- dure unti! the fuse blows. When It does blow, the last component you connected has the part on it that Is goIng bad after It warms up and Is shorting out. MALFUNCTIONING CONTROLS - - The most common problem here {fs the bad potentiometer (pot). Typlcaily, a bad pot wili cause the Image on the screen to jump when I+ reaches a certain potnt. The onty cure for thls one Is to Insta!! a new pot. \# a feature that Is operated by a switch (for example, joysticks, foot pedals, control pan- et buttons) does not operate at all, check the switch wlth a VOM or continuity tester to verlfy Its operation. if the switch does not check good, replace It, If the switch Is OK, you should suspect the Input to the switch from the PCB. In this case, get out the harness and logic schematics and check to see what kInd of Input Is supposed to be at this switch, In many cases, the Input wlll be +5 volts DC. If so, use the VOM to check Its presence with the game turned on. Normally, the switch Is used to pu}! a +5 volt DC Ine LOW to GROUND or to pul! a LOW Ine HIGH. If the PCR output Is missing, check the wire length from the PCR, if you find the stgnal at the PCR trace, the wire length or connection [fs at fault. (ft there [s no s!gnal at the PCB trace, begin exploring the PCR usIng the logic schematics and game manual. ~9-
